doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

chapter: Jazz life and the state of jazz
title: Jazz musicians as everyone else only more so
summary: Brotherhood, foxhole humor and philosophy among musicians; not geniuses on pedestals, per Johnny Griffin.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: difficult really, that I would say everybody that I ran into coming up was very accommodating. They weren’t overly friendly necessarily, but they respected the effort that you had to put in to try to be a player. And I found also their sense of humor is what got them through the life and the music, it’s kind of a foxhole sense of humor. And there are all these elements of being a jazz musician that were very typical of just being alive in the modern world, except they were heightened, they were focused up. The life of a jazz musician was such that all the kind of things that people tend to bury as they go through life were closer to the surface with these people, and they tended to be very philosophical — philosophical humor really stood out to me. So that’s what I was thinking when I said they’re like everybody else only more so because people at the time were putting jazz musicians at arm’s length. You know? Oh well they’re different, or oh that’s a different kind of person. You have to be a certain kind of person to be involved in this nightclub scene or whatever. And basically if they didn’t approach it that way they would put him on a pedestal academically. “Oh well he’s a genius” you know. Oh that’s a genius. He’s not normal. And so my thought was in the service of the music it would be helpful to find a way to let people know that this music, as Johnny Griffin used to say, “is your music, it’s my music, it’s everybody’s music.” There’s nothing that I hear that you don’t hear, we all hear the same stuff. So that’s kind of where I was coming from with that idea.
